assertions.value: The authors state, citing the adiabatic theorem (Messiah, 1999), that AQO finds the ground state of the problem Hamiltonian with high probability provided the evolution time is of order the inverse square of the minimum gap, where the minimum gap is the smallest energy gap between the ground state and first excited state along the evolution.

The minimum gap is the smallest energy gap between the ground state E0 and ﬁrst excited state E1 of the time-dependent Hamiltonian

(2010), that exact diagonalization is currently limited to about N = 30 binary variables and quantum Monte Carlo to about N = 256, and that analytic extraction of the minimum-gap scaling has been extremely difficult in practice except for a few special cases (citing Amin and Choi, 2009).

assertions.certainty_reason: Limits the paper attributes to other work, as of 2012.

They state that this quantity bounds a different quantity than the one that sets the AQO time scaling, so they assume the matrix element V01 is not extremely small, and then use the polynomial or exponential scaling of the second derivative to infer whether the AQO time complexity is polynomial or exponential in N.

This quantity is an upper bound on 2|V01|2/gmin
However, the quantity we seek for the time scaling of AQO is

assertions.reader_inference: The measured quantity bounds 2|V01|^2 / gmin, whereas the AQO runtime depends on |V01| / gmin^2. Inferring the runtime scaling therefore rests on the stated assumption about V01, so the result is a proxy, not a gap measurement.

They state this implies the AQO runtime on this data set is likely to scale at most polynomially.

assertions.value: The authors state that an exponentially small minimum gap only implies the system is unlikely to be found in its ground state if the evolution is completed in polynomial time, that due to quantum tunneling approximate solutions found by AQO can still be significantly better than those found by classical solvers, and that, citing approximability theory (Zuckerman, 2006), obtaining such approximate solutions may still be NP-hard, so finding a low-lying excited state may be difficult for classical algorithms but not for AQO.

assertions.reader_inference: The argument says AQO might give good approximate solutions; the paper does not show that AQO does so for QBoost problems. The NP-hard-to-approximate claim does not by itself show AQO can solve the approximate problem.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Aharonov et al. (2004), that adiabatic quantum optimization was shown to be polynomially equivalent to the gate model of quantum computation.
quotes: Aharonov et al. (2004) showed it to be polynomially equivalent to the gate model of quantum computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that theoretical and numeric studies of the purported computational superiority of AQO over classical computing have repeatedly given encouraging results, citing four studies listed in the reference list.
quotes: Theoretical and numeric studies of the purported computational superiority of AQO over classical computing have repeatedly given encouraging results
assertions.certainty_reason: A characterization of other work, using the word purported for the superiority.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper itself calls the superiority purported and cites four studies; the citations are in the reference list. This paper does not show a quantum speedup.

assertions.value: The authors state that benchmarking tests performed by D-Wave on their current chips (citing Rose, 2011) have indicated that they are capable of providing dramatic speedups with respect to the best known classical algorithms for certain NP-hard problems.

assertions.certainty_reason: D-Wave describes its own product; the cited source is a vendor presentation, and two authors are D-Wave staff.
assertions.reader_inference: Authors Rose and Macready are affiliated with D-Wave Systems. No benchmark data are given in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that a series of rigorous studies of the quantum mechanical properties of the D-Wave processors, culminating in a recent Nature publication (Johnson et al., 2011), have increased the excitement in the quantum computing community for this approach.
quotes: A series of rigorous studies of the quantum mechanical properties of the D-Wave processors, culminating in a recent Nature publication (Johnson et al., 2011), have increased the excitement in the quantum computing community for this approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor-affiliated description of its own processors' studies.
assertions.reader_inference: The cited Nature paper has D-Wave authors, including Rose, who is an author of this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for machine learning purposes, D-Wave's implementation of AQO can be regarded as a discrete optimization engine that accepts any problems formulated as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO), also equivalent to the Ising model and Weighted MAX-2-SAT.

assertions.certainty_reason: A description of the vendor's own product by vendor-affiliated authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The hardware experiment states a 52-variable limit for the chip used, so accepting any QUBO holds only within the chip's size and connectivity; the text does not discuss connectivity.

assertions.value: The authors state in the conclusion that QBoost offers gains over standard AdaBoost in three aspects: lower generalization error, faster classification by employing fewer weak classifiers, and smaller computational effort for training with fewer boosting iterations.
quotes: gains over standard AdaBoost in three aspects: i. lower generalization error; ii. faster classiﬁcation (employing fewer weak classiﬁers); iii. smaller computational eﬀort for training (fewer boosting iterations).
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own summary claim; the supporting measurements are mixed.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1 supports lower test error only by amounts smaller than a standard deviation, and the weak-classifier count at Q = 256 is higher than AdaBoost's. The 52-qubit experiment had a higher false negative rate than the baseline. Only the iteration count (reweightings) is clearly lower in the reported numbers.

assertions.value: The authors state that in all experiments they find the classifier constructed with discrete optimization to be significantly more compact, while the gain in accuracy is more varied.
quotes: In all experiments we ﬁnd that the classiﬁer constructed with discrete optimization is signiﬁcantly more compact.
The gain in accuracy however is more varied.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' summary claim; the reported numbers do not all support it.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1 shows more weak classifiers at Q = 256 (356.3) than AdaBoost (257.8), and the Figure 4 caption says the cumulative weak-classifier count shows no clear advantage between hardware and Tabu search. The all-experiments wording is stronger than the reported numbers.

assertions.value: The authors state that the good performance of a large-scale binary classifier trained by iterated discrete optimization, in a form amenable to AQO but solved with classical heuristics, shows it is possible to map classifier training to AQO with negative translation costs, and that any improvements by AQO to the training solution will directly increase the advantage of their algorithm over conventional approaches.
quotes: shows that it is possible to map the training of a classiﬁer to AQO with negative translation costs.
Any improvements by AQO to the solution of the training problem will directly increase the advantage of the algorithm proposed here over conventional approaches.
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion drawn by the authors, not tested directly in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not define negative translation costs; it presumably means the reformulation costs nothing in accuracy against classical boosting. The evidence is the classical-heuristic result in Table 1 and Figure 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that access to emerging hardware that realizes AQO is needed to establish the size of the gain over classical solvers, and that processors with larger qubit numbers than the 52 operational qubits of the first such experiment will be needed to see a more pronounced effect.
quotes: Access to emerging hardware that realizes AQO is needed to establish the size of the gain over classical solvers.
We already completed the ﬁrst such experiment with 52 operational qubits, but processors with larger qubit numbers will be needed in order to see a more pronounced eﬀect.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their hardware evidence in Section 8.

assertions.value: The authors state that they conclude bit-constrained learning machines can be expected to exhibit better generalization than when the weight variables are represented with higher precision, that bit-constraining can be regarded as intrinsic regularization that keeps model complexity low, and that to the best of their knowledge this has not been studied before.
quotes: Further, we conclude that bit-constrained learning machines can be expected to exhibit better generalization than what is obtained when the weight variables are represented with higher precision.
Bit-constraining can be regarded as intrinsic regularization that contributes to keeping the model complexity low.
To the best of our knowledge this has not been studied before.
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion stated without a direct experiment in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: All reported experiments use dw = 1, so the paper reports no comparison of bit depths. The conclusion rests on the bit-depth counting argument and on the QBoost-vs-AdaBoost comparisons, which also differ in regularizer and loss.

assertions.value: The authors state that treating training as an integer program renders the training problem manifestly NP-hard, thus further motivating the application of quantum algorithms that may generate better approximate solutions than classically available.
quotes: Second, this renders the training problem manifestly NP-hard, thus further motivating the application of quantum algorithms that may generate better approximate solutions than classically available.
assertions.certainty_reason: A motivational claim with no proof in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: NP-hardness of the optimization problem does not by itself imply a quantum advantage on it. The paper states no result about quantum approximation quality on these problems.

papers.title_in_file: A trustless decentralized protocol for distributed consensus of public quantum random numbers
papers.version_note: arXiv:2108.12038v1, 26 Aug 2021, dated August 30, 2021 in the text. The text layer prints Figures 5 and 6 as "Figure ??" in the Results section, holds the references only to [41], and leaves blank the node lengths m_A, m_B, m_C, m_D in the Methods sentence on the CAR threshold.
papers.what_it_is: A preprint that proposes a decentralized quantum random number generator (dQRNG) consensus protocol for N mutually distrusted parties and reports a four-party proof-of-principle experiment with entangled photon pairs from one SPDC source.

assertions.value: The authors state that they introduce the first consensus protocol that produces quantum random numbers in a decentralized environment (dQRNG), as a design and a proof-of-principle experiment, and that to their best knowledge no quantum protocol for decentralized random number generation existed before.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Results, Previous works, p.2
quotes: we formally introduce a design and proof-of-principle experiment of the first consensus protocol producing QRNs in a decentralized environment (dQRNG)
To our best knowledge, there is currently no quantum protocol for dRNG.
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority claim made by the authors, with no survey of prior work in the paper to support it.

assertions.value: The authors define the problem as how a group of mutually distrusted participants can agree on genuine random choices without a trusted third party, which they call a random number generator in a decentralized environment (dRNG), whose numbers must be unbiased, unpredictable, tamper-resistant and publicly verifiable.
quotes: in the absence of a trusted third party, how a group of mutually distrusted participants can agree on some genuine random choices for a public settlement among themselves
random number generator in a decentralized environment (dRNG) where RNs are not only unbiased, unpredictable, tamperresistant, but also publicly verifiable
assertions.certainty_reason: The Introduction defines the dRNG problem and the properties required of its numbers.

assertions.value: The authors argue that existing quantum random number generators, including the NIST beacon whose randomness is certified by the impossibility of superluminal signals, serve individual users with physical access to the device, and that remote users of a beacon must trust the beacon owner or a third party, so the beacon is a centralized source of randomness.
quotes: these demonstrations benefit only individual users that have physical access to collect QRNs directly from their own devices
Beacon users have no choice but to trust the honesty of QRNG manufacturers, or rely on verification from a third party
forcing public users to put trust in the beacon owners
assertions.certainty_reason: A motivating argument by the authors, not a result they prove or measure.

assertions.value: The authors describe the classical commit-reveal scheme for decentralized randomness, in which each participant submits a hash of a secret number and later reveals it, and state that the last participant to reveal can learn the result ahead of time, manipulate it, or refuse to reveal and end the process.
quotes: In the commit phase, each participant submits the hash of their own secret RN.
the last participant to reveal has an advantage of knowing the resulting RN ahead of time
the last revealer either manipulates the output RN or refuses to submit their secret RN, thus terminating the whole RN generation process
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of prior classical work, attributed to reference 24 and not analyzed in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that verifiable delay functions assume the malicious participant lacks specialized hardware, and that threshold digital signature methods rely on public-private key schemes with distributed key generation and are therefore vulnerable to quantum computer attacks.
quotes: that the malicious participant does not possess specialized hardware capable of cracking the inherently slow hash computation of the VDF
These methods rely on public-private keys scheme and require distributed keys generation process, hence, are vulnerable against quantum computer attacks
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about prior classical work, attributed to references 25 to 27, with no analysis in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors list six properties that they say the dQRNG protocol has: genuine (no participant controls the outcome), flexible in randomness distribution without postprocessing, decentralized, publicly verifiable, highly tolerant (outcomes are unpredictable if at least one party among N parties is honest), and quantum secured (immune to quantum computer attacks).
quotes: Genuine: no participant has control over the final outcomes.
without postprocessing, QRNs follow arbitrary probability distribution specified and agreed upon by all N parties
Highly tolerant: outcomes are unpredictable if at least one party is honest among N parties.
Quantum secured : immune to quantum computer attacks.
assertions.certainty_reason: The list states the claims; the paper supports them with an informal argument and a four-party experiment, not with a formal security proof.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that the security of the protocol is guaranteed given N minus 1 dishonest participants, and in the Analysis that the results stay unbiased and unpredictable, and all participants agree on the final result, for as long as at most k participants are malicious, where k is N minus 1.
quotes: Security of the protocol is guaranteed given (N-1) dishonest participants.
For as long as at most k participants are malicious, meaning at least 1 participants follow the protocol honestly, the results will still be unbiased and unpredictable
Let N be the number of participants, and k be (N − 1).
assertions.certainty_reason: The Correctness statement is supported only by a worked argument for four parties with one honest party; it is not proved for general N.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper states no formal security model: it gives no adversary definition, no bound on bias and no entropy accounting for the final value.

assertions.value: The authors define the notation of the protocol: N participants, k equal to N minus 1, a list R of random numbers of length l within a bounded range B, a classical list Rc from participants' choices, a quantum list Rq, a list Rqc produced by the protocol, and an aggregation function F, such as XOR or summation, agreed ahead of time so that R equals F of Rqc.
quotes: Let N be the number of participants, and k be (N − 1).
This pool would like to agree on a list of random numbers R of length l within a bounded range B.
F is a function, such as XOR operation or summation operation, agreed ahead of time by participants such that R = F (Rqc).
assertions.certainty_reason: The Construction section defines these symbols and the aggregation function.

assertions.value: The authors state that the protocol assumes a quantum network infrastructure connecting all nodes and a common, publicly agreed photon measurement basis, and that it assumes no authentication between nodes and no encryption or decryption, by quantum or classical methods, for data transfer during the protocol.
quotes: We assume the existence of a quantum network infrastructure, as described in the previous section, connecting all communication nodes.
All participants publicly agree upon a common photon measurement basis.
We do not assume any necessary authentication between nodes nor existence of any encryption and decryption
assertions.certainty_reason: The Construction section states the assumptions of the protocol.

assertions.value: The authors describe the physical layer as an entanglement source, private quantum channels between parties and an entanglement verification setup, with entangled photons passed through a beamsplitter of N to N nodes so that each party shares photon pairs with every other party, giving a number of channel pairs Pnum, and with all nodes synchronized to a common reference signal of period T.
quotes: there must be an entanglement source, private quantum channels between communication parties, and entanglement verification setup
passed through a beamsplitter of N, distributing to N
nodes such that each party shares photon pairs with
pool are synchronized to a common reference signal of period T

assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the formula for Pnum as N(N-1) over 2 in separate fragments, so the value does not restate it.

assertions.value: The paper states that in the first step, Reveal and Consensus, each participant generates and publicizes a list of random values of length m, much larger than l, each at most B, with an optional probability weight, and that the lists are combined into one list Rc whose length is m times N, with a probability density function C built from the weights.
quotes: Each participant generates and publicizes their own list of random values of length m (m >> l)
this parameter is optional
where mc = m × N
A probability density function (pdf) C is constructed by combining probability weight µi.
assertions.certainty_reason: The Construction section defines this step of the protocol.

assertions.value: The paper states that entangled photon pairs are sent to all participants, each of whom measures privately and obtains a list of photon states with indices, and that each participant then publicly reveals the results, after which entanglement verification and probability distribution verification against the pdf C are done on the correlated results of each channel pair.
quotes: Entangled photon pairs are sent to all participants. Each participant then performs photon measurement privately
Measurement results of photon states with corresponding indices are publicly revealed by each participant.
Quantum entanglement verification is performed by extracting detected photon results previous step from Pnum number of channel pairs
probability distribution verification is performed to compare with pdf C
assertions.certainty_reason: The Construction section defines these steps of the protocol.

assertions.value: The paper states that in the second consensus step the correlated results of all channel pairs are appended into a list Rq with indices I, that the quantum list is combined with the users' lists by publicly forming the intersection of I and Rc into a list of indices Ifinal, that only values with indices in Ifinal remain as Rqc, and that the output R is an aggregation function F, for example modular addition, of Rqc, computed publicly.
quotes: Quantum randomness is combined with users’ randomness by first publicly perform I ∩ Rc to assemble a new list of indices called Ifinal
the final list of random numbers is filtered so that only values with corresponding indices in Ifinal remain, called Rqc
an aggregation function F (e.g modular addition) is used to calculate publicly and can be confirmed by any participants if needed
assertions.certainty_reason: The Construction section defines these steps of the protocol.

assertions.value: The authors state that the values in Rqc are selected, by a consensus that happened before the quantum measurements were made, as a subset of the quantum random numbers harvested in the quantum process, and therefore still are quantum random numbers.
quotes: Rqc are selected as subset of QRNs harvested in the quantum process by consensus happened before quantum measurements were operated, and therefore, still are QRNs
assertions.certainty_reason: An assertion in the construction with no proof or test of it in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The selection indices depend on public values and on the revealed quantum results, so the claim that the subset is still unbiased is the point the paper's security argument must carry; the paper gives no quantitative argument for it.

assertions.value: The paper gives an argument, for four participants and one required random number in a range, with Alice the only honest party, that the final value stays unpredictable: the three dishonest parties may reveal altered or fabricated quantum results, and may agree on results that pass verification among themselves, but the combined list still holds Alice's private randomness, so Ifinal stays unpredictable and so does the output.
quotes: Assume the case of four participants Alice, Bob, Charlie, and Dave where they need to agree on one truly random number (l = 1) in the range from 0 to 6
Alice is the only one being honest (k = 3).
Rc still carries private randomness comes from Alice. Thus, the outcome indices of Ifinal = I ∩Rc remains unpredictable.
computing R = F ({rqc}) returns an unpredictable number
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal argument for one four-party case, with no probability bound; the statement for general N is not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument does not say how Alice's private randomness is a reason for Ifinal to be unpredictable when the dishonest parties choose their lists after seeing the public lists of others, and it does not treat a last-to-reveal party. The paper itself criticizes that case for commit-reveal schemes.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in the four-party case, cheaters who alter their revealed results are exposed because entanglement verification compares announced results with each other and with Alice; and that three colluding cheaters can pass verification among themselves, which makes the results of their pairs deterministic, while the pairs with Alice stay non-deterministic.
quotes: Quantum entanglement verification easily displays them because their announced results must be compared with each others and with Alice.
RqBC = RqB ∩ RqC (deterministic), RqBD = RqB ∩ RqD(deterministic), RqCD = RqC ∩ RqD(deterministic)
RqAB = RqA ∩ RqB(non-deterministic), RqAC = RqA ∩ RqC (non-deterministic), RqAD = RqA ∩ RqD(non-deterministic)
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative argument in the Analysis, with no detection probability or test shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum results reveal step runs over the classical network and is vulnerable to a digital emulation attack, in which an adversary without access to the quantum channel fabricates results that match those of every other participant, and they claim this attack neither lets the adversary know the final result beforehand nor manipulate it.
quotes: The quantum results reveal step occurs over the classical network, it is vulnerable to digital emulation attack.
Observing others revealing their results first, he then fabricates
helps him know the final random numbers result before hand nor manipulate them
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative security argument with no proof in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the protocol does not assume secure quantum authentication, an outside adversary can perform a man-in-the-middle attack and take the identity of a node with full access to its measurement results, and they claim a dishonest reveal by that adversary does not affect the unpredictability of the final result, because participants do not hide their quantum measurement results.
quotes: Since we do not assume any secure quantum authentication requirement, an outside adversary can perform MITM attack and take the identity of that node.
His dishonest reveal, if he chooses to do so, does not affect the unpredictability of the final results as proved previously.
Participants do not hide their quantum measurement results and corresponding indices
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative security argument that relies on the earlier informal argument.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says the result was proved previously; the only earlier argument is the four-party example, so this claim is no stronger than that argument.

assertions.value: The authors report an experimental setup in which an intensity-modulated continuous wave laser at 1559.67 nm pumps a PPLN waveguide for second-harmonic generation at 779.8 nm, a second PPLN waveguide generates entangled photon pairs by spontaneous parametric down-conversion, three 50/50 fiber beamsplitters send photons to four nodes, each node uses a superconducting nanowire single photon detector, and a time-to-digital converter records arrival times against a network synchronized 10 MHz reference signal.

second-harmonic generation (SHG) at 779.8 nm
a system of three 50/50 fiber beamsplitters are used to randomly transmit photons into four different nodes
superconducting nanowire single photon detector (SNSPD)
network synchronized 10 MHz reference signal

assertions.value: The authors report that the independent timing jitters of the single photon detector are 33 ps and of the time-to-digital converter 20 ps at each node, and that photon arrival times are rounded to 250 ps bins to compensate the overall timing jitter of all nodes.
quotes: Consider the independent timing jitters of the SPD (33 ps) and the TDC (20 ps) at each communication node
photon arrival times collected are rounded to 250 ps per bin-width to compensate the overall timing jitter of all nodes in the network
assertions.certainty_reason: The Figure 7 caption states the jitters and the bin width as part of the experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that three pump shapes, continuous wave, Gaussian and Rayleigh pulses, were sent into the SPDC source to give uniform, Gaussian and Rayleigh probability distributions of the quantum random numbers, and state that the correlated results of each channel pair must satisfy the designated distribution to pass the quantum results reveal step.
quotes: three different pump shapes including CW, Gaussian, and Rayleigh pulses are sent into the SPDC source, showing the versatility in probability distribution of our QRNs
Correlated QRNs of each channel pair Rqij must satisfy the designated distribution to pass the quantum results reveal step.
following uniform, gaussian, and rayleigh probability distributions
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical demonstration from one experiment, reported through figures whose data are not in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors report time-resolved coincidence peaks for all six channel pairs, state that differences in coincidence counts between pairs come from beamsplitter imperfection and from detection efficiency and timing jitter of each detector channel, and state that using one SPDC source for the whole network reduces the correlated random number rate, which they say does not affect the protocol because it produces one or a small set of numbers at a time.
quotes: Discrepancies in coincidence counts between channel pairs are due to the imperfection of beamsplitters as well as contributions by different detection efficiency and timing jitters of each SPD channel.
Using one SPDC source to distribute photon pairs to the entire network reduces the coincidence count rate or correlated QRNs rate.
even though the average Rqij rate we achieve is rather low, it does not affect the performance of the protocol
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical report from one experiment; the coincidence counts are in figures, not in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer gives no coincidence rate or CAR value, so the claim that a low rate does not matter cannot be checked against a number.

assertions.value: The authors state that the security threshold of the protocol depends on the coincidence to accidental coincidence ratio (CAR), which decides when the SPDC process ends, and give as an example a CAR threshold of 50 for the Gaussian pump shape, with generation continuing until all channel pairs reach it.
quotes: Security threshold of dQRNG protocol depends on CAR to decide when the SPDC process should end.
assuming CAR threshold is 50 for gaussian pump shape, photon pairs generation continue until all channel pairs achieve this value

assertions.value: The authors report a second case in which four parties select one winner among themselves, each with probability weight 0.25, with PRNGs generating the lists Rci; over 100 runs they report that the experimental probabilities fluctuate less than 5.28% from the theoretical 0.25, and they state this shows the protocol is unbiased.
quotes: a pool of four parties must decide who is chosen with the condition that each party equally likely has chance of being chosen (µi = 0.25)
PRNGs are used to generate list Rci in step 1 of dQRNG
The protocol is run 100 times with one party is chosen each time.
experimental results only fluctuate less than 5.28% showing the protocol is unbiased
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with simulated party lists; the paper offers no significance test behind "unbiased".
assertions.reader_inference: A spread under 5.28% of 0.25 over 100 runs is within ordinary sampling noise of a fair four-way choice, so the data would not detect a small bias.

assertions.value: The authors report that a typical sequence of 63182 correlated quantum random numbers with a uniform distribution, taken from 250 ps bins and converted to 505456 bits in an 8-bit representation, passed the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite, with P-values above the significance level 0.01.
quotes: examine this sequence using National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-22 Statistical Test Suite
NIST results of typical 63182 correlated QRNs of uniform probability distribution.
QRNs are harvested from 250 ps binwidth photon arrival times
QRNs are converted into 8-bit representation of 505456 bits and inputted into the NIST test suite
P-values greater than significance level 0.01 certifies this sequence passes the randomness threshold rigorously for standard cryptography purposes.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one sequence from one experiment; a statistical test suite cannot certify randomness.
assertions.reader_inference: The test is run on the appended quantum list Rq of correlated photon arrival times, not on the final output R of the protocol, and one sequence is tested.

assertions.value: The authors claim that their protocol avoids key distillation, quantum error correction and slow key rates, is provably random and information-theoretic secure, needs no encryption algorithm, operates without collusion given only one honest party, and avoids a conversion step when the numbers follow a non-uniform distribution.
quotes: Our dQRNG avoids the cumbersome procedures in quantum cryptography including keys distillation, quantum error correction, or slow key rates
still holds the quantum advance in being provably random and information-theoretic secure
our protocol operates without colluding given only one honest party while requiring no encryption algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: Statements by the authors in the Discussion, with no proof of information-theoretic security in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no information-theoretic security proof, and its experiment simulates the party lists with PRNGs and uses a single trusted SPDC source, so the claim of provable randomness goes beyond what the text shows.

assertions.value: The authors state that the protocol is scalable to multiple degrees of freedom of photonic states, namely polarization, spectral and spatial modes, for photon-efficient generation of quantum random numbers.
quotes: the dQRNG protocol is scalable to multiple degrees of freedom in photonics states (ie. polarization, spectral, and spatial modes ) for photon efficient generation of QRNs
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement by the authors with no experiment in the paper using these degrees of freedom.

assertions.value: The authors state that distributed applications and blockchain depend on decentralized random number generation that is kept conspiracy-resistant by classical communication techniques, and that a fast enough quantum computer would break the current methods.

It will be deleterious when a fast enough quantum computer breaks the current dRNG
assertions.certainty_reason: A motivating statement by the authors, with no analysis in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that using one SPDC source for the whole network reduces the rate of correlated random numbers, that the average rate they achieve is rather low, and that the protocol produces one or one small set of random numbers at a time on demand.

The dQRNG produces one or one small set of RNs at a time
on-demand, produces one or one set of random numbers used for decision-making on a matter involving N parties
assertions.certainty_reason: The Methods section states the low correlated-number rate and the one-number-at-a-time scope.
